newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: British minister says Saudi dissident offensive.
newsitem.headline: British minister says Saudi dissident offensive.

text.p: Britain's defence procurement minister on Saturday said a Saudi dissident exiled in London was abusing hospitality by criticising the Saudi government, but said he had a right to free speech.

"(Mohammad al-) Masari is only one of a number of dissidents who are in the United Kingdom who are in my opinion abusing the national freedoms that we have enjoyed for a very long time," James Arbuthnot told Reuters.

"The fact that our freedom of speech laws mean that people are able to say in the United Kingdom things that we find offensive is regretable to us. But we do have this tradition of freedom of speech which is also extremely dear to us."
Saudi Arabia has made veiled threats that London might lose export business because of criticism of the Saudi royal family by Masari, head of the Committee for the Defence of Legitimate Rights.

His activities enraged the Saudi royal family and when Britain's arms exporters expressed fears for their contracts the British government tried to deport him. A court ruled last year he could stay in Britain for another four years.

Britain is anxious to beat its Western rivals for arms sales to Saudi Arabia, a key weapons customer and the world's largest oil producer. British firms are in the running for several Saudi commercial and military deals.

Officials have been promoting British main battle tank maker Vickers Plc, competing with France's Giat Industries and General Dynamics Corp of the United States to supply up to 200 MBTs to the kingdom.
Arbuthnot said Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan's two-day visit to London starting on Wednesday "went extremely well." A London Foreign Office spokesman said the Masari issue was not discussed.

Asked if the Saudis were still pressing the case, Arbuthnot said: "It is no secret that some of the activities of some of the people who have begun to enjoy the hospitality of Britain are offensive to the Saudi Arabians as they are to the British".
He was speaking one day before the start of Abu Dhabi's international arms show IDEX, the biggest arms exhibition in the Middle East.
